items.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Keter, we got to be friends.

ctx.x: Yeah. She had a restaurant downstairs and a place upstairs, the same thing, where she had some music. She used to hire this trio from Port Chester, New York. It was a saxophone player, a drummer, and a bass player. They used to come down and do a couple weeks and act as the catalyst to bring people from the theater to come up there and jam. That was a way of getting people from the theater to come up there and help her to do a music thing. In that band was Keter Betts. Keter, we got to be friends.

items.title: Walter Booker and Jimmy Cobb interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995
items.q: Keter Betts got me a job with Earl Bostic’s band

ctx.x: Tell us one of the gigs that you were on when you in your own mind said I’ve arrived — I’m a player, I’m on the scene and I have a voice here.

Well I think that must have been when Keter Betts got me a job with Earl Bostic’s band and I left town. I didn’t say I’ve arrived, I say I’m leaving. Which is, so I left, from my standpoint, I’m leaving. But you know that was a pretty good thing because I didn’t know if I was ever going to get out of the town. I got to be 21 years old and I got to leave so it was great. I went to New York and then from New York I stayed in New York, which © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

that was my passage out of Washington. Not that I didn’t love Washington, I still love it. But it’s not like you’re going to make a living around there playing music. Maybe some people do but I didn’t think I could. I figured New York was the place for me. And it turned out. It worked out.

items.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996
items.q: I got Jimmy Cobb with Bostic because Bostic needed a drummer and I recommended Jimmy Cobb.

ctx.x: It didn’t take you too long before you started playing out.

I was going out a year later. The next year I went down to Washington. A saxophone player from White Plains, Carmen Leggio, had been stationed down there in the service. And when he got out he used to go jam at this club. And the lady said, “if you can get a group together I’d like for you to come in.” So he brought a drummer from Tarrytown, and a piano player from New Rochelle and myself. And we came down there, you know, green. First time away from home, we got out and the whole bit. And we came in for four…

saxophone player named Rick Henderson called me in December to see if I could come down and do a month with him in January at a club down there, sort of like a supper club, and then Bostic came to town and heard me and asked me did I want to go with him, and that’s how it went on.
